column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is a **mutation**?
column14: A change in the DNA sequence
column15: A change in the shape of a cell
column16: A protein made normally by a ribosome
column17: A trait learned during a person's life
column28: A mutation is a change in the DNA code (the sequence of nucleotides). A cell's shape, a normally made protein, and learned traits are not changes to DNA.
column29: Think about the genetic code itself. What would have to change?

column9: What causes a **frameshift** mutation?
column14: Swapping one base for another
column15: Inserting or deleting a base
column16: Flipping a chromosome piece around
column17: Changing the sugar in a nucleotide
column28: A frameshift happens when a base is inserted (added) or deleted (removed). That shifts how the bases are grouped into codons from that point on. Swapping one base is a substitution, flipping a chromosome piece is an inversion, and the sugar is the same in every nucleotide.
column29: The 'frame' is how bases are grouped in threes. What kind of change would shift every group after it?

column9: What happens in a **substitution** mutation?
column14: One extra base is added to the gene
column15: One base is removed from the gene
column16: One base is replaced by a different base
column17: A whole chromosome piece is lost
column28: In a substitution, one base is swapped for another (for example, A becomes T). The total number of bases stays the same. Adding a base is an insertion, removing one is a deletion, and losing a chromosome piece is a chromosomal deletion.
column29: 'Substitute' means to put one thing in place of another, like a substitute teacher.

column9: Which of these can damage DNA and cause mutations? Select all that apply.
column14: Cigarette smoke
column15: Visible light from a desk lamp
column16: Eating food heated in a microwave
column17: X-rays
column28: UV radiation, X-rays, and the chemicals in cigarette smoke can all damage DNA. Visible light from a lamp doesn't have enough energy to damage DNA, microwaving heats food but doesn't make it cause mutations, and loud music can hurt your hearing but doesn't change your DNA.
column29: Not every kind of light or energy damages DNA. Which ones are on your list of mutagens?

column9: A factor in the environment, like radiation or certain chemicals, that can cause a mutation is called a ___.
column28: A mutagen is anything that causes mutations ('muta-' = change, '-gen' = maker). Examples: UV light, X-rays, cigarette smoke, and some chemicals.
column29: Look back at the third cause of mutations in your notes. UV light, X-rays, and cigarette smoke are all examples of this vocabulary word.

column9: All mutations are harmful.
column28: False. Some mutations are harmful, many have no noticeable effect, and a few are helpful. Helpful mutations are part of how species evolve.
column29: Can a change in DNA ever have no effect, or even help?

column9: What usually catches and fixes mistakes made while DNA is being copied?
column14: Ligase joining Okazaki fragments
column15: RNA polymerase making mRNA
column16: Ribosomes building proteins
column17: Proofreading by DNA polymerase
column28: DNA polymerase proofreads as it copies: it checks each new base and replaces mismatches. Most copying errors are fixed this way, but a few get missed and become mutations. Ligase joins fragments, and RNA polymerase and ribosomes are part of protein synthesis.
column29: Which enzyme was adding the bases, and checks its own work?

column9: Match each disorder to the type of mutation that causes it.
column14: Sickle cell anemia :: A single-base substitution
column15: Cystic fibrosis :: A small deletion (bases are missing)
column16: Some forms of hemophilia :: An inversion (a section is flipped)
column28: Sickle cell anemia comes from a single-base substitution in the hemoglobin gene. The most common cystic fibrosis mutation is a small deletion in the CFTR gene. Some forms of hemophilia come from an inversion, where a section of DNA in a clotting-factor gene flips around.
column29: Sickle cell anemia changes just one amino acid in hemoglobin. Which mutation type changes just one base? Start there.

column9: A substitution changes one codon. Match each result to its name.
column14: Silent :: The new codon still codes for the same amino acid
column15: Missense :: The new codon codes for a different amino acid
column16: Nonsense :: The new codon becomes a stop codon
column28: Silent = no change to the protein. Missense = one amino acid is different. Nonsense = the codon becomes a stop, so the protein is cut short.
column29: 'Mis-' means wrong, as in misspell. Match that one first, then decide which of the other two leaves the protein unchanged.

column9: A mutation can be caused by a mistake made while DNA is being copied.
column28: True. Copying errors during replication (a wrong base, an extra base, or a missing base) are one main cause of mutations. Proofreading fixes most of them, but not all.
column29: Think about what could go wrong when a cell copies billions of bases.

column9: A mutation in which kind of cell can be passed on to a person's children?
column14: A sperm or egg cell
column15: A skin cell damaged by sunburn
column16: A lung cell damaged by smoking
column17: A muscle cell in the arm
column28: Only mutations in reproductive cells (sperm or egg) get passed to offspring, because those cells form the child. Mutations in body cells like skin, lung, or muscle stay in that person.
column29: Which cells actually become part of a baby?

column9: Which everyday comparison best fits a **point mutation**?
column14: Tearing a whole page out of a book
column15: A one-letter typo in a word
column16: Reading a paragraph backwards
column17: Photocopying an entire book
column28: A point mutation is like a small spelling mistake: it affects one letter (one base). Tearing out a page is like losing a whole chromosome piece, reading backwards is like an inversion, and photocopying is replication.
column29: A point mutation affects just one spot. Which comparison is that small?

column9: A section of DNA that codes for one protein is called a ___.
column28: A gene is a section of DNA with the instructions for one protein. A mutation in a gene can change that protein.
column29: It's a short word you already use when talking about inherited traits.

column9: A **deletion** removes one base from a gene. The mutation that does the opposite, putting one extra base into a gene, is called ___.
column20: insertion|insertions|an insertion|insertion mutation|an insertion mutation|insert|inserted|addition|additions|an addition|addition mutation|an addition mutation
column28: Putting in an extra base is an insertion (some books call it an addition). It is the opposite of a deletion. Because it changes how the bases are grouped into codons after it, it causes a frameshift.
column29: Look at the frameshift section of your notes. It names two mutations: one that removes a base and one that adds a base.

column9: Which kind of mutation changes a large section of DNA at once, instead of just one base?
column14: A point mutation
column15: A silent mutation
column16: A chromosomal mutation
column17: A substitution mutation
column28: Chromosomal mutations change big sections of chromosomes: pieces can be lost, copied, flipped, or moved to another chromosome. Point, silent, and substitution mutations each change a single base.
column29: Point, silent, and substitution mutations each change how many bases?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: GAA = Glu, GAG = Glu, GUA = Val, UAA = Stop. An mRNA codon changes from **GAA** to **GAG**. What type of mutation is this?
column14: Missense
column15: Nonsense
column16: Frameshift
column17: Silent
column28: GAA = Glu and GAG = Glu, so the amino acid doesn't change. That is a silent mutation. Missense would give a different amino acid, nonsense would give a stop codon, and frameshift needs an inserted or deleted base.
column29: Look up both codons. Did the amino acid change?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: CAU = His, CAC = His, CCU = Pro, UAU = Tyr. An mRNA codon changes from **CAU** to **CCU**. What type of mutation is this?
column14: Missense
column15: Silent
column16: Nonsense
column17: Frameshift
column28: CAU = His and CCU = Pro, so one amino acid is replaced by a different one. That is a missense mutation. It isn't silent (the amino acid changed), nonsense (no stop codon), or frameshift (no base was added or removed).
column29: Look up both codons. Is the new one the same amino acid, a different one, or a stop?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: UGG = Trp, UGU = Cys, UGA = Stop, CGG = Arg. An mRNA codon changes from **UGG** to **UGA**. What type of mutation is this?
column14: Silent
column15: Nonsense
column16: Missense
column17: Frameshift
column28: UGG = Trp, but UGA is a stop codon. The protein will end early at this spot, which is a nonsense mutation. Only one base was swapped, so it isn't a frameshift.
column29: Look up the new codon. Does it code for an amino acid at all?

column9: Why does a frameshift mutation usually change a protein more than a substitution does?
column14: It always turns the first codon into a stop codon
column15: It changes the DNA in every cell of the body
column16: It changes every codon after the mutation, not just one
column17: It removes the whole gene from the chromosome
column28: Adding or removing one base shifts how every later base is grouped into codons, so most amino acids after that point change. A substitution changes only one codon. Frameshifts don't always make the first codon a stop, don't happen in every cell, and don't remove the whole gene.
column29: Codons are read in groups of three. What happens to all the later groups if one base goes missing?

column9: A substitution mutation always changes the amino acid sequence of the protein.
column28: False. Many amino acids have more than one codon, so a substitution can change a codon into another codon for the same amino acid (a silent mutation). The protein stays the same.
column29: Check the codon chart: do some amino acids have more than one codon?

column9: A sentence of three-letter words models a gene: **THE BIG DOG DUG THE PIT**. After a mutation it reads **THE BGD OGD UGT HEP IT**. What type of mutation does this model?
column14: A substitution of one letter
column15: An insertion that causes a frameshift
column16: A silent mutation
column17: A deletion that causes a frameshift
column28: The I in BIG was removed, so every letter after it slid over one spot and every 'word' (codon) after that point changed. A substitution would change only one word, an insertion would add a letter, and a silent change wouldn't change the meaning.
column29: Count the letters before and after. Was a letter swapped, added, or removed?

column9: The gene sentence **THE OLD MAN SAW THE BOY** mutates to **THE OLD MAN SAW THE TOY**. What does this model?
column14: A substitution; only one word changes
column15: A deletion; every word after it changes
column16: An insertion; every word after it changes
column17: An inversion; the words are now backwards
column28: B was swapped for T, so only one 'word' (codon) changed and the rest of the sentence still reads the same. That models a substitution. Deletions and insertions shift every word after them, and an inversion would flip a section backwards.
column29: Did the number of letters change? How many words are different?

column9: Which of these could cause a mutation? Select all that apply.
column14: A person often eats hot dogs with nitrite preservatives
column15: During meiosis, a chromosome piece is lost or attached to the wrong chromosome
column16: An extra base is added by mistake during replication
column17: A person eats a meal that is high in protein
column18: A ribosome reads an mRNA to build a protein
column19: A cell copies its DNA with no errors
column28: The three main causes of mutations are errors during DNA replication (like an extra base), mistakes during meiosis (like a chromosome piece lost or attached to the wrong chromosome), and environmental factors (mutagens) like nitrite preservatives. A perfect copy changes nothing, eating protein doesn't change DNA, and reading mRNA doesn't change DNA.
column29: Think about the three causes of mutations in your notes. Which choices fit one of them?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: GAG = Glu, GUG = Val, CUC = Leu, CAC = His. In the hemoglobin gene, one DNA template triplet changes from **CTC** to **CAC**. What happens to the amino acid?
column14: Leu is replaced by His (missense)
column15: Glu is replaced by Val (missense)
column16: Nothing changes (silent)
column17: The protein stops early (nonsense)
column28: Transcribe first: CTC → GAG (Glu) and CAC → GUG (Val). One amino acid changes, which is a missense mutation; this is the mutation behind sickle cell anemia. Leu → His comes from reading the DNA as if it were mRNA.
column29: The codon chart is for mRNA. Transcribe both DNA triplets before looking them up.

column9: A chromosome's genes are in the order **A-B-C-D-E-F-G**. After a mutation, the order is **A-B-E-D-C-F-G**. What type of chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Deletion
column15: Duplication
column16: Inversion
column17: Translocation
column28: The section C-D-E flipped around to E-D-C but stayed in the same place. That is an inversion. No genes were lost (deletion), copied (duplication), or moved to another chromosome (translocation).
column29: Are any genes missing or extra? Look at the order of the middle genes.

column9: How can mutations lead to **cancer**?
column14: They make cells divide more slowly than normal
column15: They change DNA into RNA inside the nucleus
column16: They mostly happen in cells that are already cancer
column17: They can damage genes that control the cell cycle
column28: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division. Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes) can remove the 'brakes' or jam the 'gas pedal'. Cancer cells divide too much, not too slowly; mutations don't turn DNA into RNA; and mutations are what turn a normal cell into a cancer cell in the first place.
column29: Cancer cells divide out of control. Which genes would normally keep division in check?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: CUA = Leu, UUA = Leu, GAU = Asp, AAU = Asn. A DNA template triplet changes from **GAT** to **AAT**. Is this a silent, missense, or nonsense mutation? ___
column28: Transcribe first: GAT → CUA (Leu) and AAT → UUA (Leu). The amino acid is still Leu, so it's silent. Reading the DNA as mRNA (GAU = Asp, AAU = Asn) would wrongly make it look like a missense mutation.
column29: Transcribe both DNA triplets into mRNA, then look them up.

column9: While making one mRNA copy of a gene, RNA polymerase adds a wrong base. Is this a mutation?
column14: No; only the mRNA copy changed, not the DNA
column15: Yes; the mRNA error changes the gene
column16: Yes; the error will be passed to offspring
column17: No; transcription errors are fixed by ligase
column28: A mutation is a change in the DNA. A transcription error affects just one mRNA copy out of many; the gene itself still has the correct code, so nothing is passed on when the cell divides or to offspring. Ligase joins DNA fragments; it doesn't fix mRNA. RNA polymerase can make mistakes; they just aren't mutations.
column29: Where is a mutation, in the DNA or in an mRNA copy? What happens to the DNA here?

column9: A chromosome's genes are in the order **A-B-C-D-E-F-G**. After a mutation, the order is **A-B-C-F-G**. What type of chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Inversion
column15: Deletion
column16: Duplication
column17: Translocation
column28: Genes D and E are missing, so a piece of the chromosome was lost: a deletion. An inversion would flip genes, a duplication would add an extra copy, and a translocation would move genes to a different chromosome.
column29: Compare the two lists. Which genes are missing?

column9: Which is an example of a **beneficial** mutation?
column14: A mutation that causes cystic fibrosis
column15: A mutation that keeps blood from clotting after a cut
column16: A mutation that lets cells resist a virus
column17: A mutation that causes uncontrolled cell division
column28: Some mutations help, like one that lets cells resist a virus (a mutation like this protects some people from HIV). Cystic fibrosis, blood that can't clot, and uncontrolled cell division (cancer) are harmful. A protein that stops working is often harmful, but not always: that virus-resistance mutation works by turning off a protein the virus uses to get into cells.
column29: Which one gives the organism an advantage?

column9: Mutagens can be sorted into three groups: radiation, chemicals, and infectious agents. Which choice sorts all three of these mutagens correctly?
column14: X-rays: chemical; nitrites: radiation; HPV: infectious agent
column15: X-rays: infectious agent; nitrites: chemical; HPV: radiation
column16: X-rays: radiation; nitrites: infectious agent; HPV: chemical
column17: X-rays: radiation; nitrites: chemical; HPV: infectious agent
column28: X-rays (like UV light) are radiation, nitrite preservatives are chemicals, and HPV (human papillomavirus) is a virus, which makes it an infectious agent. Each of the other choices gets two of the three wrong.
column29: Start with the mutagen you're most sure about and cross out the choices that get it wrong. Then check the next one.

column9: A single-base deletion happens in the **last codon** before a gene's stop codon. Compared with the same deletion near the start of the gene, its effect is most likely:
column14: Smaller, because only the very end of the protein changes
column15: Larger, because the stop codon comes right after it
column16: The same, because every frameshift is equally harmful
column17: Zero, because deletions never change proteins
column28: A frameshift changes the codons from the mutation onward. Near the start, almost every amino acid changes. Near the end, only the last part is affected, so the protein may still mostly work. The shift can also push the stop codon out of frame, so a few extra amino acids may be added at the end, but everything before the mutation is still correct. That is why the effect is smaller than a deletion near the start. Not all frameshifts are equally harmful, and deletions do change proteins.
column29: A frameshift changes everything after it. How much protein comes after the last codon?

column9: Put these events in order, from cause to effect.
column14: UV light damages the DNA in a skin cell
column15: The protein folds differently and may not work
column16: The changed gene is transcribed into mRNA with a changed codon
column17: The base sequence of a gene changes
column18: A different amino acid is added during translation
column28: A mutagen (UV) changes the DNA. The changed gene is transcribed into a changed mRNA codon, which puts a different amino acid in the protein. A different amino acid can change how the protein folds and works.
column29: Follow the central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein.

column9: The original DNA reads **TAC-GGA-TTC**. Which mutated version shows a **deletion**?
column14: TAC-GGG-ATT-C
column15: TAC-GAT-TC
column16: TAC-GCA-TTC
column17: CTT-AGG-CAT
column28: TAC-GAT-TC has one G removed (8 bases instead of 9), and every codon after it shifts. TAC-GGG-ATT-C has an extra G (insertion), TAC-GCA-TTC has one base swapped (substitution), and CTT-AGG-CAT is the whole sequence written backwards.
column29: Count the bases in each answer. The original has 9.

column9: When a cell with a mutation divides, the mutation can be passed on to the new cells.
column28: True. The mutated DNA is copied during replication like the rest of the DNA, so both new cells get the change. (It reaches a person's children only if it's in a sperm or egg cell.)
column29: What gets copied before a cell divides?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: AUG = Met, AAA = Lys, GGG = Gly, UUU = Phe, CAA = Gln, AGG = Arg, GUU = Val. The mRNA **AUG-AAA-GGG-UUU** codes for Met-Lys-Gly-Phe. A **C** is inserted right after AUG. What is the new protein?
column14: Met-Lys-Gly-Phe
column15: Met-Gln-Gly-Phe
column16: Met-Gln-Arg-Val
column17: Met-Lys-Arg-Val
column28: The new mRNA is AUGCAAAGGGUUU. Regroup into threes: AUG-CAA-AGG-GUU (U left over). That is Met-Gln-Arg-Val. Every codon after the insertion changed, which is what a frameshift does. The other choices change only some codons or none.
column29: Write out the new mRNA with the extra C, then regroup the letters into threes from the start codon.

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: AUG = Met, GUC = Val, CAU = His, GGA = Gly, UAA = Stop, UCC = Ser, GAU = Asp. The mRNA **AUG-GUC-CAU-GGA-UAA** codes for Met-Val-His-Gly. The **G** at the start of the second codon is deleted. How does the new protein begin?
column14: Met-His-Gly
column15: Met-Val-His-Gly
column16: Met-Ser-His-Gly
column17: Met-Ser-Met-Asp
column28: The new mRNA is AUGUCCAUGGAUAA. Regroup: AUG-UCC-AUG-GAU (AA left over) = Met-Ser-Met-Asp. The stop codon UAA is lost in the shift, so the ribosome keeps going past the part shown and the protein runs on. Met-His-Gly just drops Val without regrouping the later bases, and the other choices don't shift every later codon.
column29: Remove the G, then regroup the remaining letters into threes from the start codon.

column9: Ana and Ben have the same mutation in a gene for a skin protein. Ana's mutation happened in one of her skin cells after a bad sunburn. Ben's was already in the egg cell he grew from. Which statement is most accurate?
column14: Both of them can pass the mutation on to their children
column15: Only Ana can pass it on, because her mutation is newer
column16: Only Ben has it in all his cells and can pass it on
column17: Neither can pass it on, because skin genes aren't inherited
column28: Ben's mutation was in the egg he grew from, so it was copied into every cell of his body, including the cells that make his sperm, and he can pass it on. Ana's mutation is only in skin cells: it is copied when those cells divide, but it never reaches her egg cells. How new a mutation is doesn't matter, and genes for skin proteins are inherited like any other gene; what matters is which cell the mutation is in.
column29: Which cell did each mutation start in, and which of their cells could end up in a child?

column9: A gene has 300 codons. One nonsense mutation turns **codon 5** into a stop codon. Another turns **codon 295** into a stop codon. Which is more likely to be harmful, and why?
column14: Codon 295; a stop near the end ruins the protein's final shape
column15: Codon 5; almost none of the protein would be made
column16: They are about the same; each one swaps a single base
column17: Codon 5; an early stop codon shifts the reading frame
column28: A nonsense mutation ends the protein early. At codon 5, the protein stops after just a few amino acids, so almost none of it is made and it can't work. At codon 295, the protein is almost complete and might still work. Each one swaps a single base, but where the stop lands matters. A stop codon ends translation; it doesn't shift the reading frame.
column29: A stop codon ends the protein. How much of each protein would get made?

column9: A gene's mRNA has **200 codons** for amino acids, then a stop codon. A substitution turns **codon 51** into a stop codon. How many amino acids long is the shortened protein?
column28: Translation stops at codon 51, and a stop codon adds no amino acid. Only codons 1 to 50 are translated, so the protein has 50 amino acids.
column29: Does the stop codon itself add an amino acid?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: AGA = Arg, AGG = Arg, CGA = Arg, AGU = Ser, AGC = Ser, AAA = Lys, UGA = Stop. The DNA template triplet **TCT** is transcribed to the mRNA codon AGA (Arg). A substitution changes one base of TCT. Which new DNA template triplets would make a **silent** mutation? Select all that apply.
column14: TCA
column15: TCC
column16: ACT
column17: GCT
column28: Transcribe each new template triplet: TCC → AGG and GCT → CGA both still code for Arg, so those changes are silent. TCA → AGU and TCG → AGC code for Ser (missense), TTT → AAA codes for Lys (missense), and ACT → UGA is a stop codon (nonsense). A change in the third base isn't always silent, and a change in the first base can be.
column29: The codon chart is for mRNA. Transcribe each new DNA triplet first, then look it up.

column9: People with **two** copies of the sickle cell mutation have sickle cell anemia. People with **one** copy are much less likely to get very sick from malaria. Jace says, "The sickle cell mutation is harmful, so it can never be helpful." Which response is best?
column14: He's right; a mutation that causes a disease can't also help
column15: He's wrong; sickle cell anemia isn't caused by a mutation
column16: He's right; malaria protection comes from a different gene
column17: He's wrong; the effect of a mutation can depend on the environment
column28: The same mutation can be harmful in one setting and helpful in another. Two copies cause sickle cell anemia, but one copy helps protect against malaria, so in places where malaria is common the mutation can be an advantage. The malaria protection comes from this same hemoglobin mutation, and sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation (a substitution in the hemoglobin gene).
column29: Read the stem again. Does this mutation ever give anyone an advantage? Where would that matter?

column9: In one gene, an extra base is inserted between codon 2 and codon 3. Then the **last base of codon 5** is deleted. Which codons are now read differently than in the original gene?
column14: Every codon from codon 3 to the end
column15: Only codon 3 and codon 5
column16: Only codons 3, 4, and 5
column17: None; the two changes cancel out
column28: The inserted base shifts the frame, so codons 3, 4, and 5 are grouped wrong. Removing the last base of codon 5 shifts the frame back, so codon 6 and everything after it are read normally again. Codon 4 is changed too, because it sits inside the shifted stretch, and the changes don't cancel out completely, because codons 3 to 5 are still scrambled.
column29: The insertion shifts the frame. What does removing one base later do to the frame?

column9: Use this part of the codon chart: AUG = Met, CAA = Gln, GUC = Val, UAA = Stop, AUU = Ile. The DNA template **3'-TAC-GTT-CAG-ATT-5'** codes for Met-Gln-Val. A substitution changes **GTT** to **ATT**. What happens?
column14: Missense: Gln is replaced by Ile
column15: Silent: the protein is still Met-Gln-Val
column16: Frameshift: every amino acid after Met changes
column17: Nonsense: the protein stops after Met
column28: Transcribe the new triplet: ATT → UAA, a stop codon. The protein is now just Met: a nonsense mutation. Ile (AUU) comes from reading the DNA as mRNA. Only one base was swapped, so the frame doesn't shift.
column29: Transcribe the mutated DNA triplet into mRNA, then look it up.

column9: Why are many substitutions in the **third** base of a codon silent?
column14: Codons for the same amino acid often differ only in the third base
column15: The ribosome usually skips the third base when it reads a codon
column16: The third base codes for the protein's shape, not its amino acid
column17: Proofreading fixes most changes that happen in the third base
column28: On the codon chart, codons for the same amino acid often share the first two bases (GCU, GCC, GCA, and GCG are all Ala). So changing the third base often keeps the same amino acid. The ribosome reads all three bases, the third base is part of the codon just like the other two (it doesn't code for shape), and proofreading doesn't target third bases.
column29: Many amino acids have more than one codon. Compare the four codons for Ala: GCU, GCC, GCA, GCG. Which base changes?

column9: Why are chromosomal mutations often more harmful than a single substitution?
column14: They usually turn the codons in a gene into stop codons
column15: They can change or remove many genes at once
column16: They mostly happen in reproductive cells, not body cells
column17: They change the base-pairing rules inside the cell
column28: A chromosomal mutation moves, flips, copies, or deletes a big section of a chromosome, which can hold many genes. A substitution changes one base in one gene. Chromosomal mutations don't turn a gene's codons into stops, can happen in any cell, and don't change the base-pairing rules.
column29: Compare what a substitution changes with what a chromosomal mutation changes.

column9: Chromosome 9 reads **A-B-C-D-E-F** and chromosome 22 reads **M-N-O-P-Q**. After a mutation, chromosome 9 reads **A-B-C-D-P-Q** and chromosome 22 reads **M-N-O-E-F**. What happened?
column14: Inversion: a piece flipped around on one chromosome
column15: Deletion: genes were lost from both chromosomes
column16: Translocation: pieces were swapped between two chromosomes
column17: Duplication: extra copies of genes were made
column28: E-F moved to chromosome 22 and P-Q moved to chromosome 9, so pieces were swapped between different chromosomes: a translocation. (A 9–22 translocation like this is linked to a type of leukemia.) Nothing flipped, no genes were lost, and no extra copies were made.
column29: Track where each gene ended up. Did any genes move to a different chromosome?

column9: The most common cystic fibrosis mutation deletes **three bases in a row** from the CFTR gene. What does this do to the protein?
column14: Every amino acid after the deletion changes
column15: The protein is not changed at all
column16: The protein becomes three amino acids shorter
column17: It is missing one amino acid; the rest is unchanged
column28: Three bases = one codon, so the reading frame doesn't shift. The protein is missing just one amino acid (in cystic fibrosis, one phenylalanine), but that is enough to make the CFTR protein fold wrong and not work. It isn't three amino acids shorter, because three bases make one codon, and the amino acids after the deletion don't change.
column29: How many bases are in one codon?

column9: The original DNA reads **TAC-CTT-GAG**. The mutated DNA reads **TAC-CTT-AGA-G**. What type of mutation is this: insertion, deletion, or substitution? ___
column28: The mutated strand has 10 bases instead of 9: an extra A was added after CTT, which shifts every codon after it. That is an insertion (a frameshift).
column29: Compare the two strands. What does each kind of mutation do to the number of bases?

column9: Scientists grow two groups of bacteria. Group A is exposed to UV light and grows **40** mutant colonies. Group B gets no UV and grows **3** mutant colonies. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: UV light raised the mutation rate in Group A
column15: UV light protects bacteria from getting mutations
column16: UV light stops bacteria from repairing their DNA
column17: Group B's mutations were also caused by UV light
column28: Group A (UV) had far more mutant colonies than Group B (no UV): 40 vs 3. That supports UV raising the mutation rate. The data don't test how UV works (nothing here measures DNA repair), UV clearly didn't protect the bacteria, and Group B got no UV, so its 3 mutants came from other causes, such as copying errors.
